title: Suya Beef
subtitle: Nigerian spiced peanut-dusted grilled beef skewers
excerpt: Suya is Nigeria's most famous street food -- thin strips of beef coated in a spiced peanut powder and grilled over charcoal until lightly charred. It is eaten with sliced raw onion, tomato, and extra spice powder. The peanut coating is what makes it unique.
sourceNotes: Suya is a Hausa street food that originated in northern Nigeria and spread across West Africa. The Hausa-Fulani cattle herders developed it as a portable, protein-rich food for long journeys. Today it is sold at suya spots in every Nigerian city, grilled to order over charcoal braziers.

recipe.makeAheadNotes: The suya spice mix can be made weeks ahead and stored in a jar.

content.text: The beef must be sliced very thin -- about 5mm -- so it cooks quickly. Freeze the beef for 30 minutes before slicing to make it easier to cut thinly. If using wooden skewers, soak them in water for 30 minutes before threading.

items.prepNote: use 3 tbsp peanut powder (very finely ground roasted peanuts)

content.text: Mix all the suya spice ingredients together with the grated onion and oil to make a dry paste.
Coat the beef slices thoroughly in the spice paste. Thread onto skewers, keeping the meat flat.
Leave to marinate for at least 1 hour in the fridge.
Cook under a very hot grill or on a hot griddle for 4 to 5 minutes per side until charred at the edges and cooked through. Alternatively, cook over direct charcoal for the best flavour.
Rest for 5 minutes. Serve with raw sliced onion, tomato, and a dusting of extra suya spice powder.

items.symptom: Peanut powder burns before beef is cooked
items.cause: Grill too close or heat too high
items.fix: Move the skewers further from the heat source; the peanut coating needs medium-high heat, not maximum
Aim for 5mm thick slices; cook for exactly 4 minutes per side and no more
Blend roasted peanuts in a food processor until they are almost a powder before mixing into the spice blend

content.text: Suya is Nigerian street food at its most iconic. It is sold at night, from roadside grills called suya spots, in every Nigerian city from Lagos to Abuja to Kano. The suya seller fans the charcoal with a folded newspaper while the beef sizzles and the smoke carries the smell of peanut and spice across the street.
